nameStory: Grassleaf spurge gets its name from its narrow, grass-like leaves that can fool you at first glance. The word 'spurge' comes from the old French 'espurgier,' meaning 'to purge,' referring to the medicinal (and often unpleasant) uses of plants in this family. Many spurges were once used as strong laxatives, though this practice is not recommended today!
description: Grassleaf spurge is a small, weedy annual plant that grows close to the ground in a spreading mat. It typically reaches only 6-12 inches tall but can spread wider than it is tall. This inconspicuous little plant has narrow, linear leaves that really do look remarkably similar to grass blades. Like all spurges, it produces tiny, unusual flowers and contains a milky white sap that can irritate skin.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, grass-like leaves that are smooth-edged and arranged alternately along the stem - much thinner than most spurge leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely getting taller than a foot but spreading outward in patches

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers without true petals, appearing in small clusters - they're easy to miss and don't look like typical flowers

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Break a stem and you'll see the characteristic white, milky sap that all spurges produce - sticky and potentially irritating to skin

habitat: This rare spurge is typically found in disturbed soils, waste places, and along roadsides where other vegetation is sparse. It prefers sandy or gravelly soils and full sun exposure. Given its extremely limited presence in New England (only 2 recorded observations), it's likely an occasional introduction rather than a naturalized resident.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin their low, spreading growth pattern with fresh green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their tiny, barely noticeable flowers during the warmest months.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the annual plants begin to decline, turning yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this annual dies completely, leaving only seeds to potentially germinate next year.

funFact: This spurge is so rare in New England that you're more likely to spot a shooting star than find one of these plants - with only 2 confirmed sightings, it's one of our region's botanical unicorns!
confusionNotes: The grass-like leaves make this easy to overlook entirely, as it can blend in perfectly with actual grasses. However, the alternately arranged leaves (grasses have leaves that emerge from nodes) and the milky sap when broken are dead giveaways that you're looking at a spurge, not grass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'spurges,' these plants are completely unrelated to the similarly named 'spurrey' plants. The spurge family includes everything from tiny weeds like this one to massive trees, and even the familiar Christmas poinsettia with its colorful bracts.
compareHints: Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region. Spotted spurge has oval leaves with red spots, cypress spurge has needle-like leaves but grows much taller, and most other spurges have distinctly non-grass-like foliage that won't fool you into thinking you're looking at lawn grass.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
